Found it for you, then cut it — and there was a real bug hiding under it.

Where it was: the Add income sheet. Press Add income in the sidebar of the responsive layout and it opened as an inline pane; the numbered list sat under the two choice buttons, below the fold at some widths, which is why it was easy to miss.

What was there: four layers of narration over two buttons. An eyebrow "Choose a source", the title "Add income", a subtitle "Choose W-2 or 1099 income" restating the two buttons directly beneath it, then "What happens next — 01 Choose the source type. 02 Add schedule and earnings details. 03 Return to the overview." Step 01 was the thing you were being asked to do at that moment, and step 03 is not an action. The eyebrow, the subtitle and the list are all gone.

The bug: the two buttons read "W-2 employee" and "1099 contract". ui.tsx has carried a comment for a while saying exactly why that pair is dangerous — they are categories on a tax form, somebody delivering for DoorDash does not know they are the second one, so they pick the first and lose the mileage deduction only the second one has. CLAUDE.md puts that at $1,000 of delivery pay being under $300 countable once the miles come off. The same decision was offered with the safe words in one place and the dangerous words in another.

So the pair now lives once, as SOURCE_CHOICE in domain/copy.ts, with the reasoning attached: "A job that pays me — An employer pays you, and takes tax out before you get it" and "Delivery or gig work — Driving, deliveries, or work you invoice for. Nothing is taken out." Both ui.tsx and the workspace sheet read from it.

Done, both halves, and the jitter had a cause rather than needing a device. The header collapses once you scroll, which makes the body taller, which can take the scroll away — the browser then clamps scrollTop, the header grows back, and it happens again. That loop is the glitch on a short window. Two guards: the collapse never engages unless there is more overflow than the collapse itself gives back, and once engaged it only lets go at the very top, so a few pixels of clamped scroll cannot flip it. The narrow-width half was the segmented control. It was a grid of N equal columns with N fixed by the caller; at a phone's width — where the root font is 18px, not 16 — three columns leaves about 75px a segment, so "I work here" rendered as three stacked words in a box twice the height of its neighbours. It is a wrapping row now: the caller says how many columns it would like (--seg-cols), each segment asks for that share, and no segment is ever narrower than its own label — it wraps to the next line instead. Same rule as .btn-row, and no breakpoints, for the same reason there are none there. Two more things in the same sheet. Started and Status were sharing a two-column grid, which is where the squeeze came from — half a sheet is not enough for three segments, so they sit side by side only while both fit. And the eyebrow was clamped to max-h-5 while still being allowed to wrap, so "A job that pays me" put its second line on top of the title; nothing clamps it while it is open now, the clamp is only what closes it.

thread.text: Done in src/review/ReviewProvider.tsx. A new `replyTo` state carries the intention, because `openRow` alone cannot tell two different acts apart: clicking a row is 'let me read this' and must not move the page under the reader or take the keyboard, while pressing Reply is 'I want to type now' and has to arrive somewhere. Only the two Reply paths set it — the queue card's button and the R key. The effect that watches it travels to the row (skipped when the row is already in view, so opening one under the pointer does not throw it to the top of the list), then checks the box against the list it sits in and pulls it in only if the thread was long enough to leave it below the fold, then focuses it with preventScroll so focus does not fight the scrolling. Measured on a 1471px list in a 458px window: from the bottom of the list, Reply lands at scrollTop 195 with the box in frame and the caret in it; clicking a visible row moves the list zero pixels and leaves focus alone.

Both scrolls are instant rather than smooth, and that is the fix rather than a preference: with `behavior: 'smooth'` the second move measured a rectangle while the first was still animating, so it read a position that was about to change and then fought the animation that produced it. Landed instantly they compose into one jump. Worth recording — anything else in this console that scrolls twice in a row will hit the same thing.

thread.text: Done in src/review/ReviewProvider.tsx. Three parts. Done. src/components/settingsModel.ts now holds the shape — the four sections in order (Account, Appearance, Your data, The rules), the row ids each one contains, and one label per row. Both screens read it: src/components/SettingsPanel.tsx maps sections to its Tailwind rows, src/components/calc20/SettingsSheet.tsx maps the same sections to its tabs. A layout declares the rows it can actually draw and sectionsFor() drops the rest, so a section left empty never becomes a heading or a tab. That is how the two screens keep their differences without either of them carrying a list of exceptions — only calc20 has the glass slider and the clear-one-year button, only the shared panel has the palette swatches, and neither file says so.

calc20's tabs were Status / Appearance / Data / About and are now the four shared sections. It lands on Appearance rather than the first tab: the order says Account goes first, but nobody opens Settings to look at a consent switch and a legal document.

The steps are now in src/state/cloudSyncGuard.ts — consent before on, typed DELETE before off, and the backup downloaded before the delete rather than offered after it — and both screens run them: src/components/SettingsPanel.tsx draws them in its own primitives, src/components/calc20/SettingsSheet.tsx keeps its .warning panels and now calls the shared hook instead of its own copy of the state machine.

task-review-sourceline-producer.label: anchor.sourceLine is read but never written
task-review-sourceline-producer.reason: Design audit of the review console itself, 2026-09-02. Full case: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/f1124b40-39fa-458b-b5b0-ba8a29243104 Counts verified against the 222-note corpus on 2026-09-02.
task-review-sourceline-producer.comment: types.ts declares anchor.sourceLine with the longest comment in the file, and vite.review-plugin.ts:79 reads it to decide whether an element is still in the source. Nothing anywhere writes it: 0 of 222 notes carry one. That is why found is 'unknown' on 184 of 222 notes, why the report is full of '(near line 78, unverified)', and why 'done is never asserted, only earned' is earned against evidence the tool never collected. The fix is one function beside the fiber read that already produces `source`: read the line the anchor points at and store it trimmed. Smallest change in the review stack, largest effect — it is the difference between a queue you trust and one you re-check by hand.

audit-review-two-state-machines.label: Two state machines still describe one note
audit-review-two-state-machines.reason: Design audit of the review console itself, 2026-09-02. Full case: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/f1124b40-39fa-458b-b5b0-ba8a29243104 Counts verified against the 222-note corpus on 2026-09-02.
audit-review-two-state-machines.comment: ReviewLane (5 lanes, LANE_NAME, laneOf) in types.ts and NoteState (8 states, STATE_NAME, stateOf) in state.ts are both live. `status` is typed as the lane, documented in REVIEW-NOTES.md as the state, and stores lane values, which stateOf() translates on every read with a heuristic that can silently reclassify done as sent. state.ts's own header already diagnoses this — it produced 49 phantom-done notes — but the thing it replaced was never deleted. Add verdict (4) and the derived Do column (8 verbs, 6 hues) and one note wears four overlapping taxonomies: 61 labels across 13 enumerations. Proposal: collapse to three states, because the state IS whose move it is — Yours / Sent / Closed. Delete ReviewLane, verdict, the DO map and actOf(). The data supports it: the 'second' lane is used by 0 of 222 notes, and all 178 closed notes are 'done' — not one 'later', not one 'wontDo'. The taxonomy is also already leaking: certainty is typed 'sure' | 'likely' | 'hunch' and five notes carry 'certain', a fourth value nothing defines and nothing renders. With four taxonomies and three writers, that is not a mistake anyone made — it is what happens.

task-review-delete-dead-subsystems.label: Trays, screenshots, placement and A/B serve 3 notes between them
task-review-delete-dead-subsystems.reason: Design audit of the review console itself, 2026-09-02. Full case: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/f1124b40-39fa-458b-b5b0-ba8a29243104 Counts verified against the 222-note corpus on 2026-09-02.
task-review-delete-dead-subsystems.comment: Usage across the 222 notes on file: stow 2, tray 1, members 1, choice/options 1, shots 3, placement 0. That is stow.ts, TrayEdge, TraySettings, TraySort, ReviewPlacement, the four edge shelves and their drag handling, the screenshot composer, ReviewVariants.tsx and the 'variants' mode — roughly 900 lines and five vocabulary words serving seven notes between them. None of it is bad work; the variant switcher is a good idea that went unused. Pure subtraction: nothing in the notes file depends on them, `hidden` already covers 'take it off the page and see', and version control is the archive. Do this second, after sourceLine.

audit-review-scope-tab-lies.label: The board says 'You are clear' with 127 notes waiting
audit-review-scope-tab-lies.reason: Design audit of the review console itself, 2026-09-02. Full case: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/f1124b40-39fa-458b-b5b0-ba8a29243104
audit-review-scope-tab-lies.comment: The Notes panel opens scoped to 'This screen'. On a fresh load of the plan layout that showed 6 notes and the message 'You are clear', with 127 notes sitting on other layouts and a small grey link at the bottom offering to show them. A queue that hides its own backlog by default is worse than no queue. Proposal: drop the scope tabs entirely and always show everything, grouped by whose move it is. The reviewer's working set is four to eight things; 'notes on this screen' is a filter, not a default.

task-review-strip-board-chrome.label: 39 interactive targets to service 4 notes
task-review-strip-board-chrome.reason: Design audit of the review console itself, 2026-09-02. Full case: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/f1124b40-39fa-458b-b5b0-ba8a29243104
task-review-strip-board-chrome.comment: Counted off the live rail with four notes on screen. Before the first note: scope tabs, walkthrough button, row-select mode, collapse-all, a seven-item keyboard legend, five filter chips, a progress line, three column headers, two group bands — eleven controls. Then seven affordances per row: checkbox, Do chip, open, state pill, Locate, visibility switch, Dismiss. The filter strip also mixes two taxonomies — Comments and Reply are Do verbs, Redesign is a user tag. Proposal: one column, no scope tabs, no filter strip, no bulk select, no collapse-all, no wide mode (it hides the app under review behind the tool reviewing it). A row is a state dot, a label, the sentence and where it lives, with three actions: Locate, Hide, Reply. The Do column goes — the sentence already says what is being asked, better than any of the eight verbs derived from it.

task-review-dock-furniture.label: Three dock edges, panel reorder and column splitters, all state and no decision
task-review-dock-furniture.reason: Design audit of the review console itself, 2026-09-02. Full case: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/f1124b40-39fa-458b-b5b0-ba8a29243104
task-review-dock-furniture.comment: 621 lines carrying three dock edges, drag grips to reorder panels, per-panel folds, draggable column splitters, wide mode and per-screen size clamping — for a rail that is only ever docked right. Four modes (off / audit / pick / variants) should be two: pointing, or not. Tags should go from the 8 in use to the four that carry — cut, move, reword, redesign. Open question rather than a recommendation: MobileDock.tsx is a second implementation of the same rooms, so every feature is built twice. Only 236 lines, so the cost is the duplication tax rather than the file — worth keeping only if you genuinely review on a handset rather than at an emulated width. Your call.

task-review-split-console.reason: Design audit of the review console itself, 2026-09-02. Full case: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/f1124b40-39fa-458b-b5b0-ba8a29243104
task-review-split-console.comment: ReviewProvider.tsx is 4,275 lines, of which ReviewConsole spans 311-4232 as a single component holding 44 useState and about 20 useRef. Split it into the three surfaces the tool actually has: capture (hover, select, comment, anchor), list (the queue), handoff (the Markdown report and Copy for AI). Do this LAST, once there is less of it to split — after sourceLine, the deletions and the state collapse, the remaining console should be around 1,800 lines and the split is then mechanical rather than archaeological.

audit-review-vocabulary-weight.label: That the console needs a dictionary is the finding
audit-review-vocabulary-weight.reason: Design audit of the review console itself, 2026-09-02. Full case: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/f1124b40-39fa-458b-b5b0-ba8a29243104
audit-review-vocabulary-weight.comment: VOCABULARY.md is 10.8 KB and most of it is a changelog of word collisions already fixed — Keep/Dismiss, Find it/Locate, Show/Put back/Restore, Note/Notes/Noted, Done the button vs Done the lane. Every entry is a real fix, and the file is well written. But a tool whose words need a dictionary has too many words. Once the state collapse in audit-review-two-state-machines lands, this file should shrink to about a page: three states, three row actions, four tags, two modes. When the surface is that small, the UI is the dictionary. Keep the file — it is the right instinct — but let its length be the metric it reports on.

task-content-audit-2026-09.label: Content audit: every user-visible string, graded against four questions
task-content-audit-2026-09.reason:
A full content pass across every layout, asked for as "tighten content meanings so that the person reading will not wonder, what does this text mean? give less room for error".

The finding worth keeping is that most of what was wrong was not a bad word — it was a missing one. Four questions a label has to answer, and the failures each one prevents:

thread.text: Done. src/index.css adds --good-text / --warn-text / --info-text as one named contract — the ink that goes ON the matching -soft fill — in both themes, and repoints --warn-foreground at --warn-text so its eight existing call sites keep working against one value rather than two. Measured in the running app: good on good-soft 4.68 -> 7.94 (light) and 5.24 -> 8.60 (dark); info on info-soft 5.06 -> 8.45 and 4.99 -> 8.19; warn was already 8.41 and is unchanged. `chip-good` / `chip-info` / `chip-warn` now all take the ink. Call sites moved: src/components/SafetyHero.tsx (the Safe badge), src/components/TrackerV3.tsx, src/components/StreamSheet.tsx (x2), src/components/MonthGrid.tsx, src/components/Onboarding.tsx, src/components/ui.tsx.

task-border-tiers-base-theme.label: Base theme gets the border tiers the pg-* palette already had
task-border-tiers-base-theme.reason: index.css had one --border. The three shells each wanted a lighter one for chrome edges and were mixing it by hand as border-border/70 and border-border/60, and nothing had an emphasis tier at all — the pg-* palette has had --pg-border-strong for a while and this one did not, so the scrollbar was the only chrome on the page nobody could theme.

thread.text: Done. src/index.css adds --border-soft and --border-strong in both themes, exposed as --color-border-soft / --color-border-strong. --border-soft is what `app-bar` draws its edge with, replacing four hand-mixed alpha slices; --border-strong themes the scrollbar (scrollbar-width: thin plus the ::-webkit-scrollbar trio, added in @layer base). Verified in the running app in both themes.

task-dim-tier-declined.label: The reference's third ink tier, deliberately not adopted
task-dim-tier-declined.reason:
The Improve CSS Design export carries --color-dim (#8a9e87) as a third text tier below muted, used for axis end-caps and redundant hints. It measures about 2.9:1 on its own background. I did not bring it across: this app's reader is disabled, often low-vision, and often reading a cheap phone in daylight, and a sub-3:1 text tier is a regression for them whatever it does for the mockup. Writing it down so the next pass does not read the export and adopt it as an oversight.

If a third tier is wanted, it should be a WEIGHT or a SIZE step, not a lightness step.

task-two-scales-overlay-vs-index.label: overlay.css and index.css disagree about radius
task-two-scales-overlay-vs-index.reason:
src/styles/overlay.css is imported last in src/main.tsx, so it wins, and it re-declares `.panel { border-radius: var(--pg-radius-xl) }` = 1rem while src/index.css sets --radius-xl: 1.25rem. Every panel on every layout is drawn at the pg-* scale, not the base one, and neither file says so. The same file also sets `.panel { box-shadow: none }` globally, which is the right answer under the device constraint but means index.css's `@utility panel { box-shadow: var(--shadow-card) }` is dead code that reads as live.

One of the two is wrong. Found while adding the app-bar and nav-item rules to index.css — I did not touch it, because picking the winner changes every layout and is a decision, not a cleanup.

task-overlay-adds-blur-to-pg-chrome.label: The polish overlay ADDS a backdrop-filter to payguard's sticky chrome
task-overlay-adds-blur-to-pg-chrome.reason:
src/styles/overlay.css section 5 puts `backdrop-filter: saturate(1.4) blur(10px)` on .pg-topbar, .pg-sticky-page and .pg-sticky-surface — the sticky chrome of payguard, ledger, workrecord and calc20. backdrop-filter is on the banned list at the top of CLAUDE.md, and the overlay is loaded last in src/main.tsx so it wins over anything those layouts say for themselves. The overlay's own header says it is additive polish; this is the one rule in it that the device constraint forbids.

I did not change it. The classic/sidebar/workspace family and horizon are now flat and opaque (see [[task-app-bar-one-strip]]), but the pg-* family is a different theme with its own tokens and four layouts hanging off it, and its polish layer is in flight — flattening it is a decision someone should take on purpose, not a side effect of a pass on the other family.

Found while flattening the base-theme app bars.

task-one-palette-five-variants.label: One palette, five variants, one setting
task-one-palette-five-variants.reason:
"Lets merge all themes into proper theme with variant options, right now its crazy I cant keep up."

What was there: five variant names (paper, slate, ledger, carbon, calc20) declared across nine overlapping selector blocks in payguard.css and three more in ledger.css, each a partial patch over paper. A palette is 36 tokens and not one variant set all 36 — slate set 16, ledger 19, carbon 27, calc20 32 — so whatever a variant left out it inherited from paper silently. ledger.css declared its own values for three of the same names under --lg-*, gave 'slate' and 'ledger' one shared block so two options identical there and different everywhere else, and opted out of the app's light/dark toggle entirely. And three UiState fields (ledgerTheme, payguardTheme, workRecordTheme) held one decision, two of them indexing the same CSS, so keeping payguard and workrecord alike meant setting the same value twice.

thread.text:
Done. src/styles/palette.css is the only file that chooses a colour now: two axes (variant = hue and paper, answering all 23 choices every time; ink = light/dark, which elevation follows rather than the variant), with carbon declaring itself dark in both modes in one line instead of in JavaScript. Generated by resolving the old cascade, so the five variants render as they did — verified token by token in the running app, all 36 tokens across all 10 variant/mode combinations, --t-* and --pg-* agreeing everywhere.

src/styles/payguard.css lost 155 lines (nine palette blocks became one aliasing block, no values in it) and src/styles/ledger.css 25. Neither file's call sites moved — ~1200 of them. src/state/storage.ts has one `palette` field with a migration that prefers payguardTheme, then ledgerTheme, then workRecordTheme, because workRecordTheme mostly carries an untouched default rather than a choice; verified against a pre-merge record. Call sites: src/App.tsx, src/components/ledger/TrackerLedger.tsx, src/components/payguard/TrackerPayGuard.tsx, src/components/payguard/PayGuardShell.tsx, src/components/workrecord/TrackerWorkRecord.tsx, src/review/anchor.ts, index.html.

Two things this fixed on the way: --t-topbar was color-mix(), which an old WebView drops whole, leaving payguard's and workrecord's top bar with no fill; and ledger now answers the app's dark mode, which it never did.

Guard: scripts/theme-check.mjs, wired into `npm run build` before tsc. It fails on a missing choice, on anything outside palette.css setting a --t-*, and on a literal colour inside an aliasing block. Both failure modes tested by breaking them on purpose.

task-palette-defaults-lost-calc20-plate.label: Palette defaults must be zero-specificity
task-palette-defaults-lost-calc20-plate.reason: First cut of palette.css put calc20's dark top-bar plate in the shape section and the derived default (--t-topbar: var(--t-surface)) two sections below it. Same specificity, so the later one won and calc20's bar came out white — the whole identity of that variant is a dark ink plate under a sky-blue rule. Caught in the running app, not by the check.

thread.text: Fixed in src/styles/palette.css: every default block is written :where([data-palette]), which is zero-specificity, so a variant's own block wins wherever it sits in the file. scripts/theme-check.mjs gained an OVERRIDABLE set naming the shape tokens and the three topbar tokens, which are the only names a variant may set outside its 23 choices — anything else has to exist on paper first, or it is a colour only one variant has and nobody can find. Verified: calc20's plate resolves to oklch(22% 0.045 258) again on both workrecord and payguard.

task-palette-base-theme.label: The base theme and calc20 still have their own palettes
task-palette-base-theme.reason:
The merge covers the three layouts that already had variants — payguard, workrecord, ledger. src/index.css (classic, v2, workspace, horizon, plan, pocket) and src/styles/calc20.css still declare their own light/dark palettes and ignore `palette` entirely, so picking Midnight moves three layouts and not the other seven. index.css is oklch and semantically different (--background/--foreground/--muted-foreground against --t-bg/--t-fg/--t-fg-muted); calc20.css is 105 tokens plus a --glass-* system.

I stopped here on purpose. Mapping index.css onto the palette changes how classic, v2 and the workspace look completely — from the lime-and-emerald oklch system to the merged hex one — and that is a decision to see before it is locked in, not a cleanup to slip into a refactor. The contract, the check and the one setting are in place, so the remaining work is per-file and each file can land on its own.

task-palette-status-colours-same-in-dark.label: Status colours are identical in light and dark
task-palette-status-colours-same-in-dark.reason:
Resolving the old cascade showed that --t-safe / --t-warn / --t-over / --t-twp / --t-info / --t-w2 / --t-se / --t-ring / --t-head do not change between paper/light and paper/dark — only the surfaces and inks do. So the same mid-lightness green that reads on white is being used on #111a24, and the soft-fill pairings have no dark form at all. This is the same gap the base theme had before [[task-status-ink-tier]] gave it --good-text / --warn-text / --info-text.

Carried across as-is rather than fixed, because the merge was meant to be faithful. Worth measuring now that every variant's values are in one file and can be checked as a set.

audit-dom-node-budget.label: DOM node budget — measured, not guessed
audit-dom-node-budget.reason: Asked to plan a refactor toward "minimum necessary divs". Measured the live DOM at 390px on every layout before changing anything, and the premise did not hold.

thread.text: Measured on a 390px viewport, two jobs x twelve months of data, focus mode off, scope=year. Total app nodes / visible / mounted-but-display:none / divs: pocket 21/21/0/4 - horizon 83/83/0/7 - classic 161/161/0/21 - v2 167/147/20/20 - responsive 226/163/63/27 - plan 246/246/0/6 - calc20 385/372/13/140 - ledger 434/425/9/154 - workrecord 442/428/14/169 - payguard 641/200/441/260. Structural audit of payguard and workrecord: 0 flat pass-through wrappers, 0 nested single-child div chains, 0-4 empty divs. Of workrecord's 169 divs: 45 flex containers with 2+ children, 16 grid, 56 painted single-child surfaces, 23 positioned/overflow, 19 text leaves. There is no wrapper bloat to delete - every div is a flex/grid container or a painted surface. The only real excess is payguard mounting all three mobile tabs (see task-payguard-mobile-tabs-mount). Conclusion: do not run a div-reduction pass across the layouts. Node counts are all under the 800 Lighthouse warning once payguard is fixed, and the app has no tests, so a structural pass would be verified only by eye across 10 layouts x 5 palettes x 2 ink modes.

Workstream A is done - see task-payguard-mobile-tabs-mount. PayGuard on a phone is 205 nodes where it was 641, which puts every layout in the table under 450. The recommendation stands for the rest: no div-reduction pass. The next best DOM work is the content the review queue already asks to cut (payguard-overview-stats, payguard-hero-ytd, payguard-year-chart), which removes whole subtrees and improves the screens at the same time. One thing found while verifying, worth knowing before anyone tries to check responsive behaviour here: Chrome device emulation re-lays the page out at a new width without firing matchMedia change or window resize, so any component that branches on useIsWide will hold its old answer until you reload. It is a harness artifact, not a bug - noted at the top of src/viewport.ts.

task-payguard-mobile-tabs-mount.label: PayGuard mounts all three mobile tabs

anchor.sourceLine: const showSection = (owner: MobileTab) => wide || mobileTab === owner;

task-payguard-mobile-tabs-mount.reason: DOM measurement pass (see audit-dom-node-budget). On a phone PayGuard mounts 641 nodes and hides 441 of them with display:none - 69% of the layout is the two inactive tabs.

thread.text: sectionVisibility() switches mobile tabs with a CSS class, so the overview block (122 nodes) and the jobs block (314 nodes) stay mounted on a phone while the analysis tab is showing. display:none costs nothing to paint, but those nodes are still built on first render and re-diffed by React on every keystroke in the job editor - on a cheap Android that is the one measurable DOM cost in the app. Fix: keep the sm+ behaviour (all sections visible) and, below sm, render only the active section - a matchMedia('(min-width: 640px)') hook feeding a wide ? <Section/> : mobileTab === owner ? <Section/> : null gate at lines 321, 333 and 345. focusStream() and openAnalysis() set the tab before their requestAnimationFrame scroll, so the target exists by the time they look for it. Not started.

Done. src/components/payguard/TrackerPayGuard.tsx - sectionVisibility() is gone; showSection() now gates the three sections at lines 336, 348 and 361 so below 640px only the active tab is rendered, and at 640px and up all three render as before. The breakpoint comes from useIsWide(WIDE_MIN) in the new src/viewport.ts, which is the generic half of calc20/useIsWide.ts moved out to the root beside theme.ts - calc20 re-exports it, so its five call sites are untouched. Measured after, 390px viewport, two jobs x twelve months: 641 nodes -> 205 on the Months tab, 398 on Jobs, 206 on Your limit; mounted-and-hidden went 441 -> 5. Visible node count is unchanged at 200, so nothing left the screen. Verified all three tabs render and switch, pg-job-<id> and pg-analysis still exist when focusStream() and openAnalysis() look for them in their rAF, no console errors, and a fresh mount at 1100px still renders all three sections with the bottom nav hidden. Typecheck passes.

task-all-css-one-palette.label: Every stylesheet on one palette, each with an override layer
task-all-css-one-palette.reason:
"I feel like all css should be, and all themes have their own override layer can you do that" — extending [[task-one-palette-five-variants]] from the three layouts that already had variants to the whole app.

Five stylesheets were picking their own colours: index.css (39 + 39 dark, a green oklch family nothing else shared), payguard.css, ledger.css, calc20.css and plan.css. chrome.css then answered the same 23-token contract six times over because each family spelled its colours differently. overlay.css re-declared the paper palette a sixth time at :root and, loading last, silently won — its --pg-radius-xl of 1rem beat index.css's 1.25rem for every .panel in the app.

thread.text:
Done. src/styles/palette.css grew from 23 choices to 39: the status families are now symmetric (safe/warn/over/info each with -soft, -text and -fg), plus accent/accent-fg and primary/primary-fg. The 8 derived roles were computed per variant rather than hand-picked — a hue-preserving tint for each -soft, then the ink darkened or lightened until it cleared 7:1 on it — and every one of the 45 resulting pairs was measured: worst 7.0:1 for ink-on-soft, worst 4.54:1 for ink-on-solid. primary/primary-fg are chosen rather than derived, because a call-to-action colour is a pick; paper keeps the base theme's existing pair.

Bridged: src/index.css (the .dark block is gone entirely — dark is an axis of the palette, so there was nothing left for it to say), src/styles/plan.css, src/styles/chrome.css (six answers to one contract became one; 118 colour declarations to 21), src/styles/overlay.css (section 0 deleted outright — the problem it existed for cannot recur). Override layers, each marked @override with a reason: plan's sprite ink, bevels, gilt and parchment; chrome's scrim; overlay's two-tier elevation; calc20's dark-plate status hues.

data-palette moved from four layout roots to <html>, which is also what fixed the sign-in, terms and onboarding screens resolving no palette at all. The picker now appears on every layout instead of three — SettingsPanel reads ui.palette from the tracker rather than taking a prop pair that seven layouts never passed.

Verified in the running app: all 39 tokens across all 10 variant/mode combinations resolve and agree with their bridged names, and classic, plan, pocket, horizon, calc20, ledger, workrecord, payguard and v2 were each opened across palettes. npm run build is green.

task-carbon-was-dark-without-dark-class.label: A single-ink palette has to force the dark class
task-carbon-was-dark-without-dark-class.reason: carbon is dark in both ink modes — it declares color-scheme: dark and has no light form. But `.dark` on <html> followed UiState.theme only, so carbon with theme:'light' gave a dark page with every .dark-keyed rule switched off: plan kept its light parchment and light bevels on a black page, and pocket has about thirty such rules.

thread.text:
Fixed in src/theme.ts. applyTheme now asks the stylesheet whether the palette on <html> is single-ink — it clears the .dark class and the inline color-scheme first, because both are things we set last time and would otherwise be read back as the palette's own answer — and ORs that into the dark decision. Reading it back rather than checking for the name means another single-ink palette needs no change here.

index.html's pre-paint script cannot ask, because it runs before any stylesheet has parsed, so it carries a SINGLE_INK list. That is a duplicate on purpose, and scripts/theme-check.mjs fails if it stops matching the palettes that declare themselves dark — tested by breaking it.

task-plan-title-plate-black-on-black.label: Plan's title plates were black on black in dark mode
task-plan-title-plate-black-on-black.reason: `.pl-plate` and the sheet header stamp their text in --parch on a --px-ink ground. --px-ink is near-black in both ink modes, but --parch is also a panel BACKGROUND and goes dark when the page does, so every title plate in the layout — "I GOT PAID", "TRIAL WORK MONTHS" — was black on black under dark ink. Present in the code before this pass; the palette merge made dark reachable enough on this layout to notice.

thread.text: Fixed in src/styles/plan.css: a --plate-fg in plan's override layer, near-white in both modes, because the plate's ground is fixed dark and its ink must be too. Used by .pl-plate and the sheet header's h2. Verified under carbon.

task-calc20-pocket-not-on-palette.label: calc20 and pocket are the two files left
task-calc20-pocket-not-on-palette.reason:
The two stylesheets still picking their own colours.

calc20.css: 101 colours across html.pg-calc20 and [data-theme='dark'], plus a --glass-* system with its own axis. It is a self-contained design system that already handles its own light/dark, so it works — it just does not follow `palette`, and picking Midnight leaves it alone.

pocket.css: no tokens at all. Its colours are hardcoded inside about thirty `.dark .pk-*` rules, so it follows the ink axis but not the variant. Migrating it means rewriting rules rather than a token block, which is why it is separate from the rest of this pass.

Both are listed in `npm run theme:check`'s PENDING output so the debt stays visible without blocking a build. Remove a name from that set when it migrates.

task-color-mix-left-in-derived-layers.label: 64 color-mix() uses left, mostly now replaceable
task-color-mix-left-in-derived-layers.reason:
`npm run theme:check` reports them: 35 in calc20.css, 26 in payguard.css, 3 in ledger.css. color-mix() is on the banned list at the top of CLAUDE.md because an old Android WebView drops the whole declaration, so a soft fill silently becomes transparent and a hairline border disappears.

Most of payguard's are now redundant: --pg-safe-bg is color-mix(safe 10%, transparent) and the palette has a real --t-safe-soft for every variant. The ones without an equivalent are w2, se and twp, which have a base colour but no soft/text family — the same asymmetry that caused the original drift, one level down.

Not fixed in this pass because the -border variants (30–32% tints) have no palette equivalent either, and mapping them to the full status colour is a visible change to four layouts that should be looked at rather than slipped in.
